full_judgment:
MA Rashid J: The above Rules Nisi except the one in Writ Petition No. 1513 of 2006 were issued against a common order dated 10-2-2003 passed by the Appeal Officer under rule 31 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 hereinafter referred to as the Rules, 1955, which set aside his earlier orders dated 5-12-1999; 18-11-1999; 22-11-1999; 22-12-1999 and 15-5-2000 dismissing the appeals of respondent No.2, Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate. In Writ Petition No. 1513 of 2006, the Rule was issued against similar order dated 20-5-2003 of said Appeal Officer. 

 5. After the wholesale acquisition under section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, in short, the SAT Act, rent receiving interest of aforesaid land receiver was acquired and Rahima Dad Khan became 'Malik' directly under the Government and his name was accordingly, recorded in Review Khatian in 161 and 164 dated 24-1-1959, Annexures D and D1. 

 15. Of the respondents, respondent No. 1 represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Land and respondent No.2, Bhawal Raj Court of Wards represented by a manager appeared and filed affidavits-in-opposition. In the affidavit of respondent No.1, it is stated that said respondent No. 2 made an application to the Settlement Officer for cancellation of the order passed by the Appeal Officer under Rule 31 of the Rules, 1955 and for rehearing of the appeals. The Settlement Officer accordingly cancelled the aforesaid appeal order under Rule 42 of said Rules, 1955 and appointed Mr Moshiur Rahman (respondent No. 7) Appeal Officer and Charge Officer by his memo dated 18-12-02 for disposal of the appeals afresh. Respondent No. 8 Appeal Officer heard the appeals and allowed the same and asked to record the name of respondent No.2, which was approved by the Settlement Officer on 6-3-2003. The Appeal Officer decided the appeals in accordance with the guidelines issued by respondent No.3, Secretary vide his letter dated 10-10-02. 

 16. The petitioners managed to record their names in respect of the case land. As per direction of the Ministry of Land issued time to time, the Directorate of Land Records and Survey updated the maps and records of the land in the country. The petitioners did not acquire any right or title on the basis of the documents annexed to the writ petition from said Court of Wards Estate, which was holder of intermediary interest. 

 17. In the affidavit-in-opposition of said respondent No.2, the statements made in the writ petition were denied only. In the supplementary affidavit-in- opposition, it is however, stated that the suit land along with other land originally belonged to the Bhawal Raj Estate owned by Rajendra Narayan Roy Chowdhury. In 1901, he died leaving three sons, namely, Kumar Ronendra Narayan Roy Chowdhury, Kumar Ramendra Narayan Roy Chowdhury and Kumar Rabindra Narayan Roy Chowdhury. First Kumar died in 1910, second Kumar in 1909 and third Kumar in 1913. All of them died childless. 

 18. Under section 5 of the Court of Wards Act, 1879, the Court of Wards assumed the charge of the entire Bhawal Raj Estate in 1913 and has since then been managing the Estate. The Court of Wards was under the Board of Revenue up to 1973. In the year 1989, the Land Reforms Board Act was promulgated and by office order dated 23-5-1989, the management of the Estate came under the Land Reforms Board, Annexure- Y and Y1. 

 20. The present Rule was obtained after two years of the impugned order. In the meantime, new record was finally published in the Gazette. In sup- port a copy of attested Khatian No. 194 was annexed as Annexure- Y (4) but no Gazette could be produced. After final publication of the record-of- rights, an aggrieved person may institute a suit before the Land Survey Tribunal created under section 145A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 by the Act IX of2004 and the writ petition is not maintainable. 

 21. It is further stated that petitioner No. 1 already instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 96 of 2005 for permanent injunction in the First Court of Senior Assistant Judge at Dhaka and ultimately, has withdrawn the same with leave of the Court. Respondent No. 2 also instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 188 of 2006 in the Fourth Court of Joint District Judge at Dhaka for a decree declaring the SA record-of-rights and RS record-of-rights void, illegal, collusive, baseless and also that respondent No.2 is the owner in possession of the case land. 

 22. By filing an affidavit-in-reply on behalf of the petitioners, it is stated that on the prayer of the defendants further proceeding of Title Suit No. 188 of 2006 was stayed by an order dated 9-7-06 of this Division in Civil Revision Case No. 2447 of2007. 

 24. He submitted that after the wholesale acquisition under section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 of the receiving interest of said Bhawal Raj Court of Wards and Radha Shayam Banik, the petitioners became 'Malik' directly under the Government, which is evident by the gazette notifications, Annexure Sand S(1) to the writ petition and long continuous possession by the petitioners admittedly evidenced by SA record-of- rights and RS record-of-rights, respondent No.2 has got no right or interest in the land and objections raised by respondent No.2 against the draft record of rights.in Mahanagar Survey were all through rejected but at the behest of respondent No.7, Settlement Officer, the Appeal Officer most illegally allowed the appeals after rehearing of them and termed such lawful possession of the petitioners as 'Possession by Force'. 

 25. He submitted that in view of section 8A of the Court of Wards Act, 1879 and President's Order No. 90 of 1972, respondent No.2 has got no right to challenge the record-of-rights of the land which already stood acquired under section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 Annexure-S and after publication of the Compensation Assessment rolls finally published under section 46E(3) of said Act, Annexure S I. In support, he cited Bangladesh vs Sree Sree Modan Gopal Jeo Begraha 33 DLR (AD) 13 and Anwara Begum vs Noorjahan Begum 27 DLR (AD) 109. 

 26. He submitted that after disposal of an appeal by the Appeal Officer under Rule 31 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, the Settlement Officer has got no jurisdiction under Rule 42A and/or 44 of said Rules, 1955 to set aside such appellate order and direct the Appeal Officer to rehear the appeal under said Rule 31 and such Appeal Officer acted beyond his jurisdiction in rehearing such appeal and allowing the same. In support; he cited an unreported decision dated 6-3-2007 and 7-3-2007 of this Division in the case of Azmiri Begum vs Bangladesh. 

 28. Mr TH Khan, learned Senior Advocate, read the relevant provisions of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 and submitted that the Settlement Officer rightly exercised his power under Rules 42 and 42A thereof in cancelling the appellate order and asked the Appeal Officer to hear the appeals afresh, and after such rehearing in presence of the parties, impugned order was passed long back and if anybody is aggrieved by such order, he would have to take his grievance before the Land Survey Tribunal established under Chapter XVIIA of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (Act XXVIII of 1951), which was inserted by section 2 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 2004 (Act IX of 2004). 

 30. It is not disputed that the record-of-rights prepared under section 143 and revised under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 were finally published in the names of the petitioners in respect of the land in question. After final publication, under section 144A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (Act XXVIII of 1951), every entry in such record-of-rights prepared or revised under section 144 shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry, and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved by evidence to be incorrect. Such record-of-rights becomes binding upon all parties including the Government. The provisions for correction of such record-of- rights are now omitted. 

 32. Then, after dismissal of the appeals by the Appellate Officer, respondent No. 2 on 14-7-2002 made an application to the Settlement Officer at Dhaka for hearing of the appeals under Rule 42A of the Rules, 1955. Under the signature of the Secretary of the Ministry of Land a circular was also circulated in respect of recording of the Government Khas land and land of Court of Wards. In the circular, the revenue authority is directed to examine the SA and RS record-of-rights by following the CS that is Cadastral Survey, record-of-rights in respect of recording the Khas land and the land of the Court of Wards. It is also stated that in case where SA record and RS record was not prepared in accordance with the rules and/or decision of the appropriate authority, it would not be proper in the present survey to have the reflection of continuity of SA record-of-rights and RS record-of-rights only. In such cases, the CS record shall have to be followed in the preparation of the Khatians and maps. Copy of said application and circular are annexed to the affidavit-in-opposition of said respondent No. 2 in Writ Petition No. 1512 of 2006. 

 35. It is already noted that after final publication of a record-of-rights and revised record-of- rights, every entry in such record-of-rights shall be presumed to be correct until such presumption is proved by evidence to be incorrect. The presumption arising out of such record-of-rights is of course rebuttable, which could only be possible in a properly constituted suit. It is also true that such presumption arising out of a record-of-rights relates to the time when it was prepared and with the passage of time, as the state of things starts changing and such presumption also loses its weight. But it must be remembered that a finally prepared and published record-of-rights takes precedence over the last record-of-rights. Moreover, the entries made in the CS record-of-rights which was prepared from 1917 to 1922 cannot be expected to be the same in 2002 and to override the SA record-of-rights and revised record of rights. 

 37. With regard to the second question, it is needless to say that an appeal is the creature of a statue and right to appeal therefore cannot be assumed by any authority under any law unless it is so provided. In the scheme of revision of a record-of-rights under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 there are various stages laid down in the Rules, 1955. 

 40. Chapter VIII of said Rules, 1955 deals with general power of Revenue Officer in revising record-of-rights under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Rule 42 gives special power to a Revenue Officer appointed with additional designation of Settlement Officer to direct at any time before the publication of the final record-of-rights that any portion of the proceedings referred to in rules 28 to 32 in respect of any district, part of a district or local area shall be cancelled and the proceedings shall be taken up fresh from such stage as he may direct. Similarly, such Settlement Officer is empowered under Rule 42A upon an application or receipt of an Official Report to correct any entry that has been procured by fraud in record- of-rights before final publication, and after consulting the relevant records and making such other enquiries as he deems necessary, to direct excision of the fraudulent entry and his act in doing so shall not be open to an appeal. At the same time, the Revenue Officer shall make the correct entry after hearing the parties and record his finding in a formal proceeding for the purpose of future reference. But none of such powers under Rule 42 or 42A of the Rules, 1955 appears to empower such Settlement Officer to sit and/or act as an appellate authority over an appellate order passed under Rule 31 and set aside such appellate order or direct the Appellate Officer to hear an appeal afresh in respect of a particular holding. Nor the Appellate Officer is empowered to rehear an appeal which was finally disposed by him. The Settlement Officer therefore most illegally cancelled the appellate orders and compelled the Appellate Officer to hear the appeals afresh. 

 43. Such conclusion of the Appellate Officer as arrived by the impugned order therefore, must be held to be based on surmise and conjecture and more precisely on the instructions of the Secretary vide circular dated 10-11-2002. He fell in serious error in law in holding that possession in the lands in question, mutations after transfer of the lands, SA record-of-rights and RS record-of-rights as finally published in the names of the petitioners did not reflect the state of things as recorded in the CS record-of-rights. 

 44. In revision of a record-of-rights under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the particulars to be included, amongst others, are enumerated in Rule 26 of the Rules, 1955. Such particulars relate to the present state of things and not to the things which existed in 1922. Moreover, it is neither possible nor expected for such a recording officer to transfer title since 1922. Practically, such record-of-rights is to be prepared on the basis of present possession duly backed by documents of title only. It must be remembered that such record-of-rights does not confer any title though it is a very good evidence of possessory rights. The Appellate Officer definitely failed in the discharge of his duty in not considering the registered documents in support of transfers of the lands in question since 1929. Which carries statutory presumption of correctness and also the statutory presumption under section 144A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 attaching to the finally published SA record-of- rights and RS record- of-rights in the names of the petitioners. 

 45. In the famous case of Pramatha Nath Chowdhury vs Kamir MandalI7 DLR (SC) 392, the Supreme Court of Pakistan held on such statutory presumption arising out of section 103B of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 (Act VIII of 1885) : 

 "The presumption that attaches to a record of right under section 103B of the Bengal Tenancy Act is only this, that the entry in the record of right represents the correct state of affairs On the date that it was prepared. Whether that state of affairs continued even afterwards is not a presumption which arises under this section but under section 114 of the Evidence Act, and its probative value diminishes progressively with the lapse of time. The older the record the less is the presumption value. This is a matter, therefore, of proof and it merely has the effect of shifting the onus upon the other side. It is certainly not a conclusive proof." 

 47. Respondent No.2 is stated to be Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate represented by manager with office in 141-143 Motijheel Commercial Area at Dhaka. As said respondent filed objections against the draft publication of the recent record-of- rights, it was so impleaded in the Rules. Section 5 of said Act clearly states that the Board of Land Administration shall be the Court of Wards for the territories to which the Act extends. Besides such Court of Wards, no other Court of Wards could be conceived in the Act. We also could not find the existence of such Act in the Indian Code. The Act might have served out the purpose. Disqualification of the proprietors of the estates both in respect of property and person ceased to exist long ago. 

 50. He submitted that after acquisition of rent receiving interest of the concerned estates, the tenants of the Bhawal Raj Estate were no more tenants under them and became "Malik" directly under the Government. Article 143(c) of the Constitution is not applicable in the case of present record-of-rights and the circular dated 10-11-2002 is illegal and any action taken thereupon must be set aside. 

 51. Lastly, he submitted that management of the properties of disqualified owners by the Court of Wards is a matter of long past. Either they have overcome their disqualification in the meantime or have died leaving heirs to inherit the estates. A relevant question therefore arises, if there is at all any necessity or scope for such Court of Wards to function in Bangladesh. That is a matter which is best to be left to be considered and decided by the legislature. But the country has suffered the "Enemy Property" and "Abandoned Property" and the litigations enough to take a lesson. He however, cautioned against any strong observation from this Division in respect of the two Courts of Wards, which are still functioning in the country and the attention of proper quarters might be drawn. 

 52. But one cannot prevent the law to take its own course. After the publication of general notification No. 2773 dated 26-2-52 under section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and the notification No. 3126 dated 27-2-56 declaring the Compensation Assessment-rolls under section 43(2) read with section 46 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, all rent-receiving interest stood acquired and the tenants of any such rent-receivers became "Malik" directly under the Government and all non-retainable khas land vested in the Government. 

 53. In the case of Bangladesh vs Sree Sree Madan Gopal Jew 33 DLR (AD) 13, the Appellate Division set at rest all controversy regarding the impact of such wholesale acquisition as under: 

 "It is to be further observed that it is now well settled on the authority of Jalil Ahmed vs Province of East Pakistan: 19 DLR 106 decided by a Special Bench and affirmed by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in Tanvir Ahmed Siddiky vs Province of East Pakistan: 20 DLR (SC) 144 = PLD 1968 SC 185 that on the publication of the notification under section 3 of the Act, all rent receiving interests including that of Debuttor and Waqf Estate stood acquired and all non-retainable khas land also stood vested in the Government. 

 54. Section 8A of the Court of Wards Act, 1879 provides that if the rent-receiving interests of a ward in any estate under the charge of the Court are acquired under the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, then, notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Act, the remaining properties of such ward including khas lands under the charge of the Court shall continue to remain under its charge and shall be managed in accordance with the provisions of this Act, as if such Ward was a disqualified proprietor of an estate. Section 8A was inserted by section 2 of the East Bengal Court of Wards (Amendment) Act, 1952 (Act X of 1952). Then, under section 2A of the Bangladesh Laws (Amendment) Ordinance, 1976 (Ordinance IX of 1976) the Commissioners shall, until otherwise specifically provided for by law, possess and exercise within the several districts comprised in their respective divisions the powers and authority now vested in the Courts of Wards, subject to the control and direction of the Government and to such restrictions and provisions as the Government may prescribe. 

 55. In view of section 8A of the Act and section 2A of said Ordinance, the retainable Khas land of a ward of the erstwhile proprietors vested in the Government and the Government shall possess and manage such land on behalf of such ward and no person save the Government can be allowed to represent any of the wards of the Bhawal Raj Estate, if any survived, in respect of any retainable khas land only. How much retainable khas land still belongs to which of the wards of said estate could not be ascertained, we understand such survey was never made. It may be noted that it is misleading to say Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate since no such Court of Wards finds its existence in the Act. Similarly, whereabouts of the manager could not be ascertained. Who made whom manager could not be made clear. Nor any authority could be placed before us on behalf of the manager to represent the estate. We also wanted to know from Mr TH Khan about the present legal position of so-called manager representing respondent No.2 and he could not give any positive answer. 

 57. The Government must know its limitation and may be therefore, filed no objection to the publication of draft record-of-rights. Some manager on behalf of the Bhawal Raj Estate filed the objections and appeals. Every time, we were told, whenever revision of record-of-rights commenced, so-called manager put up objections against such record-of- rights. If the objections of such manager are heeded to then few record-of-rights in the city of Dhaka would be immune from such objections. 

 58. On the technical ground on maintainability of the writ petition, when confronted, MTH Khan failed to produce any gazette notification of final publication of the recent record-of-rights. He said due to the pendency of the Rules, the record-of- rights could not be finally published. Under section 145A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, when the Government would establish the Land Survey Tribunal only after final publication of last revised record-of-rights prepared under section 144 and after establishment of such Tribunals, any suit challenging correctness of the last revised record-of-rights shall lie in such Tribunal. 

 59. Mr Nurul Amin and Abul Quashem adopted the arguments of Mr TH Khan. Mr Quashem however insisted for decision on title. We can only say if any person on behalf of so-called Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate or Bhawal Raj Estate is still aggrieved he can go to a Civil Court of competent jurisdiction for vindication. He does not have any remedy under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. They have already exercised their choice by institution of Title Suit No. 188 of2006 in the 4th Court of Joint District Judge at Dhaka for declaration of title in certain lands and they may pursue the cause there. 

 62. Impugned orders dated 10-2-2003 and 20- 5-2003 are hereby declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and, as such, of no legal effect, and first appellate orders dismissing the appeals of respondent No. 2 presented under Rule 3 I of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 are accordingly, restored.
